title: Axial attack of hydride on a cyclohexanone
subtitle: The Bürgi–Dunitz angle and a locked ring: small hydrides attack axially

reactants.caption: 4-tert-butylcyclohexanone + lithium aluminium hydride
reactants.learnerPrompt: Hydride adds to the locked ketone. Draw the addition.
hintTiers: Which bond of AlH₄⁻ holds the electrons, and which atom of the ketone is electron-poor?
An Al–H bonding pair becomes a new C–H bond to the carbonyl carbon, and the C=O π pair moves onto oxygen. Two arrows.
Al–H bond → new C–H bond to the carbonyl carbon; C=O π bond → lone pair on oxygen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: The carbonyl oxygen is electron-rich. Hydride goes to the electron-poor carbonyl carbon.
The C=O π electrons move towards oxygen, the electronegative atom, not onto carbon.
Hydrogen is more electronegative than aluminium: the Al–H pair travels with the hydrogen, as hydride.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right: hydride attacks the carbonyl carbon. That carbon now has five bonds: move the C=O π pair.

alkoxide.caption: lithium alkoxide, hydrogen added from the axial direction (OH ends up equatorial)

alkoxide-and-acid.caption: lithium alkoxide + H₃O⁺ (work-up)
hintTiers: The alkoxide oxygen is a strong base. Which species is the acid?
The oxygen lone pair takes a proton from H₃O⁺, and that O–H bonding pair stays on water's oxygen. Two arrows.
Alkoxide oxygen lone pair → new O–H bond to a proton of H₃O⁺; that O–H bond → lone pair on water's oxygen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: That carbon now has four σ bonds and no leaving group. H₃O⁺ is the acid here.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Good: the alkoxide takes a proton from H₃O⁺. Where does the O–H bonding pair go?

steps.explanationAfterStep: The hydride approaches the π* orbital at the Bürgi–Dunitz angle, about 107° to the C=O. From the axial direction it passes close to the axial hydrogens two carbons away, a small steric cost. From the equatorial direction the forming C–H bond would be eclipsed with the C–H bonds of the neighbouring carbons (torsional strain). For a small hydride the torsional strain matters more, so it attacks axially and the oxygen is pushed equatorial. The app does not check stereochemistry yet: the drawing shows only which atoms are bonded.

steps.caption: Dilute aqueous acid is added once the reduction is over (work-up); the aluminium salts are removed.

steps.explanationAfterStep: Protonation gives the alcohol without touching the ring carbon, so the trans : cis ratio of about 9 : 1 is the one set by the hydride's approach.

mechanismSummary: The tert-butyl group locks the ring, so the two faces of the ketone are different: axial and equatorial. A nucleophile attacks a carbonyl along the Bürgi–Dunitz trajectory, about 107° to the C=O, to overlap with the π* orbital. Small hydride donors such as LiAlH₄ attack from the axial direction, which avoids eclipsing the neighbouring axial C–H bonds, and the oxygen ends up equatorial: about 90% trans-4-tert-butylcyclohexanol. A bulky donor such as L-Selectride cannot pass the axial hydrogens on the same face and attacks equatorially, giving mainly the cis alcohol with an axial OH. The app does not check stereochemistry yet: the drawing shows only which atoms are bonded.
